qs.q: An experiment examines transport kinetics across a cell membrane for a specific amino acid. At high extracellular concentrations, the transport rate reaches a plateau. What does this saturation behavior indicate?
o: Endocytosis running at maximum vesicular rates
Simple passive diffusion limited by the bilayer
Carrier-mediated transport via a finite number
Pore formation limited by physical channel size
Osmotic equilibrium halting net movement rates
qs.e: Saturation kinetics indicate that transport occurs via saturable carrier proteins with a finite number of available binding sites.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with a steroid-secreting adrenal cortical adenoma undergoes molecular evaluation of her hormone receptor signaling pathways. What is the initial intracellular event that occurs immediately after the steroid hormone crosses the cell membrane?
o: Phosphorylation of membrane-bound tyrosine kinase domains by the hormone
Direct covalent cross-linking with a hormone response element on DNA
Binding to an intracellular receptor located in the cytoplasm or nucleus
Immediate recruitment of adenylyl cyclase to generate intracellular cAMP
qs.e: Lipid-soluble steroid hormones cross the cell membrane by simple diffusion and bind directly to intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus. Membrane tyrosine phosphorylation and adenylyl cyclase activation are pathways utilized by peptide hormones.

qs.q: Which major class of antifungal medications acts by binding to ergosterol and creating pores in the fungal cell membrane?
o: Polyenes acting by binding ergosterol and creating pores
Echinocandins acting by disrupting fungal cell walls
Azoles acting by inhibiting ergosterol synthesis enzymes
Allylamines acting by blocking squalene epoxidase pathways
qs.e: Polyenes such as amphotericin B bind directly to ergosterol to poke holes in the fungal membrane. Azoles, by contrast, inhibit the synthesis of ergosterol rather than binding to it directly.

qs.q: Which of the following statements regarding the fungal cell membrane is correct?
o: It is made of chitin exclusively
It contains peptidoglycan as a component
It is primarily composed of cholesterol
qs.e: Ergosterol is the major component of the fungal cell membrane and a target for many antifungals. Chitin is found in the cell wall, not the membrane, and fungi do not use cholesterol or peptidoglycan.
qs.s: Medical Mycology Fundamentals: Fungi, Antifungal Drugs & More: MCQs

qs.q: Which antifungal drug class exerts its primary pharmacologic target by binding to cell membrane ergosterol?
qs.e: Amphotericin B targets cell membrane ergosterol to disrupt fungal cellular integrity. Echinocandins target cell wall glucans, whereas flucytosine and griseofulvin target nucleic acids and microtubules.
qs.s: Medical Virology: Adenoviruses, Hemorrhagic Fever & Viral Receptors: MCQs

qs.q: Polyene antifungals such as Amphotericin B exert their fungicidal mode of action by directly interacting with a specific lipid component of the fungal cell membrane to form lethal pores. What is this target lipid?
qs.e: Polyenes bind directly to ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that cause cell contents to leak out and result in cell death. Chitin is a structural component of the fungal cell wall.

qs.q: A pediatric hematologist is reviewing the geographic distribution of red blood cell membrane disorders. In which demographic group is hereditary elliptocytosis found with significantly higher prevalence?
o: Patients with severe dietary vitamin B12 and folate deficiency
Populations residing permanently at extreme high-altitude locations
Individuals with ancestral lineage from malaria-endemic regions
Newborns with concurrent congenital metabolic storage disorders
qs.e: Hereditary elliptocytosis occurs worldwide and in all ethnic groups but is more common in patients with ancestry linked to areas of endemic malaria. This distribution mirrors selective evolutionary advantages similar to sickle cell trait.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a painless testicular tumor. Histological examination reveals sheets of uniform polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm and distinct cell membranes, accompanied by a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate in the stroma. Which tumor marker may be elevated in 10% of these cases?
qs.e: The histological description is classic for a seminoma, which can present with elevated hCG in 10% of patients. AFP elevation is instead indicative of a yolk sac component or mixed tumor.

ai.title: Cell Membrane Structure and Clinical Significance
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: The cell membrane controls entry and exit of substances, hosts receptors for pathogens, and its dysfunction underlies many tropical diseases. Clinicians must recognise how membrane changes affect diagnosis and treatment, especially when resources are limited.

sections.p: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins, cholesterol, and glycolipids. It provides a selective barrier, maintains ionic gradients, and mediates cell signalling and pathogen entry.
b: Phospholipid bilayer: amphipathic molecules with hydrophilic heads outward.
Integral proteins: channels, transporters, receptors (e.g., CD4, CCR5).
Peripheral proteins: cytoskeletal attachment, signalling cascades.

sections.h: Features of the membrane relevant to infection
sections.p: Pathogens exploit membrane receptors to attach, fuse, or be endocytosed. In low‑resource settings, HIV‑1, malaria parasites, and bacterial toxins are classic examples.
b: HIV‑1 gp120 binds CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4 on T‑cells and macrophages.
Plasmodium falciparum merozoites use glycophorin A on red cells for invasion.
Bacterial exotoxins (e.g., diphtheria toxin) bind specific membrane proteins to enter cells.

sections.p: While the membrane itself is not a disease, its alteration contributes to pathology such as HIV infection, malaria severe anemia, and hereditary membrane disorders like sickle‑cell disease.
b: HIV infection – loss of CD4+ T cells via membrane fusion.
Severe malaria – parasite‑induced rigidity of red‑cell membranes causing microvascular obstruction.
Sickle‑cell disease – polymerised HbS stiffens red‑cell membrane, reducing deformability.

sections.p: Identify membrane‑related pathology through clinical clues, simple bedside tests, and targeted laboratory investigations.
b: When rapid tests are unavailable, use clinical staging (WHO HIV stage) and treat empirically.
If microscopy is not possible, rely on rapid diagnostic tests for malaria.

t.b: Confirms HIV infection; a positive result explains CD4‑mediated membrane entry.
Detects malaria parasites and sickled red cells; shows membrane‑related deformity.
Low K⁺ indicates hyperpolarisation of cell membranes, explaining arrhythmias in hypokalaemia.

sections.p: Therapy targets the pathogen and supports membrane function. In low‑resource hospitals, drug choice is guided by availability, safety, and interaction with membrane processes.
b: If artemisinin is unavailable, use quinine with careful monitoring for cardiotoxicity.
When antiretrovirals are out of stock, prioritize NNRTI‑based regimens that are cheap and robust.

t.b: Corrects hypokalaemia; restores normal membrane potential and reduces arrhythmia risk.

t.a: Blood transfusion for severe malaria anemia
t.b: Improves oxygen delivery; replaces rigid infected red cells with functional membranes.

sections.p: Focus on how membrane biology translates to bedside findings and management decisions.
b: Remember CD4 + CCR5 are the key receptors for HIV entry; CCR5 blockers (e.g., maraviroc) are used only when CCR5‑tropic virus is confirmed.
In malaria, a peripheral smear showing >5 % parasitaemia signals severe disease needing IV artesunate.
Hypokalaemia signs (muscle weakness, ECG flattening of T waves) reflect altered membrane excitability.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe malaria with >5 % parasitaemia or organ dysfunction
Acute HIV seroconversion with high fever and lymphadenopathy

faq.q: Why does HIV need both CD4 and a co‑receptor?
faq.a: Binding CD4 anchors the virus; the co‑receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) triggers gp41 conformational change for membrane fusion.

faq.q: How does hypokalaemia affect the cell membrane?
faq.a: Low extracellular K⁺ hyperpolarises the membrane, reducing excitability and predisposing to arrhythmias.
Yes; drugs that alter ion channels (e.g., quinine) can cause cardiac conduction problems, so monitor ECG when possible.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with fever, lymphadenopathy, and a positive rapid HIV test presents with a new rash – what membrane‑related mechanism explains the rash and what is the next step? — Explain HIV‑mediated immune activation via CD4 loss and start antiretroviral therapy while assessing for opportunistic infections.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area has a hemoglobin of 5 g/dL and a peripheral smear showing 6 % Plasmodium falciparum – which membrane property is causing the severe anemia and how should you manage? — Describe parasite‑induced rigidity of red‑cell membranes and give IV artesunate plus blood transfusion.

A patient with known sickle‑cell disease presents with chest pain and low oxygen saturation – which membrane abnormality is most relevant and what immediate investigation is required? — Stiffened red‑cell membranes cause vaso‑occlusion; obtain chest X‑ray and consider acute chest syndrome.

In a low‑resource clinic, a patient with severe vomiting has an ECG showing flattened T waves – what electrolyte disturbance is likely and why does it matter for the membrane? — Hypokalaemia; it hyperpolarises cardiac cell membranes, risking arrhythmia – give IV potassium.

You suspect bacterial toxin‑mediated disease but lack toxin assays – how can membrane knowledge guide empiric therapy? — Recognise that exotoxins bind specific membrane receptors; start appropriate antitoxin or antibiotics covering likely organisms.

A pregnant woman from a rural area tests HIV‑positive; why might a CCR5 antagonist be unsuitable in this setting? — CCR5 antagonists require tropism testing, often unavailable, and are costly; NNRTI‑based regimens are preferred.

During a malaria outbreak, rapid tests are out of stock – what bedside sign suggests severe disease needing referral? — Presence of altered mental status, respiratory distress, or >5 % parasitaemia on smear.

A patient on quinine develops QT prolongation – which membrane channel is affected and what alternative drug can be used? — Quinidine blocks cardiac potassium channels; switch to artemisinin‑based therapy if available.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a step‑by‑step physical exam reveal how the cell membrane contributes to the presenting illness, especially in HIV, malaria and sickle‑cell disease.
b: Ask about recent fever, chills, rigors and travel to malaria‑endemic areas; note any recent insect bites or exposure to fresh water.
Inquire about HIV risk factors, previous testing, antiretroviral availability and adherence; ask about opportunistic infections.
Ask about sickle‑cell crises: pain pattern, triggers, recent transfusions, and baseline hemoglobin.
Ask about drug history (quinine, antimalarials, ART, herbal remedies) that may affect membrane channels or electrolytes.
Ask about pregnancy, diabetes, renal or hepatic disease that modify membrane stability or drug metabolism.

t.b: Look for pallor, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, rash or edema; presence suggests hemolysis, infection or immune activation but cannot define membrane pathology.
Identify malaria parasites, sickled cells or elliptocytes; high parasitaemia (>5 %) indicates severe malaria, sickled cells confirm hemoglobinopathy, but smear cannot quantify membrane rigidity.
Assess microvascular perfusion; delayed refill may reflect rigid red‑cell membranes in severe malaria or vaso‑occlusion in sickle‑cell disease, but does not differentiate cause.

t.a: Neuromuscular exam (strength, reflexes, ECG bedside strip)
t.b: Detect hypokalaemia‑related membrane excitability (muscle weakness, flattened T waves); bedside ECG cannot give exact potassium level, only suggests membrane depolarisation.
Enlarged spleen supports malaria or hemolysis; cannot determine whether membrane damage is parasite‑driven or hereditary.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Laboratory and point‑of‑care tests answer specific questions about membrane‑related disease severity and guide treatment when resources are limited.
b: Rapid HIV test (initial) – positive requires confirmatory second rapid test per national algorithm; a single positive does not confirm infection.
Malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) – detects HRP2 or pLDH; a positive result confirms infection, but a negative RDT with high clinical suspicion warrants microscopy or repeat testing.
Full blood count – low hemoglobin with high reticulocyte count suggests hemolysis; a left‑shifted neutrophil count may indicate bacterial toxin exposure.
Serum electrolytes – low potassium (<3.5 mmol/L) explains flattened T waves; corrects membrane excitability.

t.a: Confirmatory HIV test (second rapid or ELISA)
t.b: Answers whether the patient is truly HIV positive; a concordant positive confirms infection and triggers WHO staging.
Answers immune status; CD4 <200 cells/µL indicates advanced disease, higher risk of opportunistic infections, and need for prophylaxis.
Answers parasite species and density; >5 % infected red cells or >200 000/µL indicates severe malaria requiring IV artesunate.
Answers tissue hypoxia from microvascular obstruction; >2 mmol/L suggests severe malaria or sepsis, prompting aggressive support.
Answers membrane excitability; <3.5 mmol/L explains ECG changes, requires replacement; if unavailable, treat empirically based on ECG.

t.a: Peripheral blood smear for sickle cells
t.b: Answers presence of sickle‑cell disease or trait; >30 % sickled cells in peripheral smear confirms disease, guiding crisis management.
Answers renal involvement in severe malaria or HIV; positive protein may indicate glomerular injury but cannot specify membrane cause.

sections.p: Combine bedside findings with investigations to place the patient into recognized disease categories that dictate management priorities.
b: HIV infection – confirmed by two rapid tests; stage using WHO clinical stage I–IV; CD4 count refines stage when available.
Severe malaria – parasitaemia >5 % or >200 000/µL, cerebral involvement, severe anaemia (Hb < 5 g/dL), renal failure, or lactate >2 mmol/L.
Sickle‑cell crisis – acute pain ≥2 sites, Hb drop >2 g/dL from baseline, new infiltrates on chest X‑ray, or acute chest syndrome criteria.
Hypokalaemia‑induced membrane dysfunction – serum K⁺ <3.5 mmol/L with ECG flattening or U‑waves; severity graded mild (3.0‑3.5), moderate (2.5‑3.0), severe (<2.5).

sections.p: Several other disorders mimic membrane‑related presentations; a focused table helps separate them using key clinical clues and simple tests.

t.b: Presents with fever, hypotension, rash; stool culture or toxin PCR confirms; lack of specific membrane receptor involvement; bedside: no malaria parasites, no sickled cells.
Triggers: certain drugs, infections; peripheral smear shows bite cells, Heinz bodies; normal malaria smear; Coombs test negative; history of drug exposure helps differentiate.
Chronic anaemia, skeletal changes, microcytosis; smear shows target cells, not sickled cells; ferritin elevated; no acute membrane rigidity.
ECG shows peaked T waves, not flattened; serum K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L; history of renal disease; distinguishes from hypokalaemia‑related membrane dysfunction.

sections.p: A practical ladder for disorders where cell‑membrane pathology is central – severe malaria, HIV infection, and toxin‑mediated disease – tailored to low‑resource hospitals.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give high‑flow oxygen if SpO2 < 90 % and correct severe hypoglycaemia.
2. Obtain rapid bedside diagnostics (HIV rapid test algorithm, malaria rapid diagnostic test, thick/thin smear if available, clinical toxin suspicion).
3. Start empiric antimalarial (artemether‑lumefantrine) if malaria test unavailable but severe signs present (parasitaemia ≥ 5 %, cerebral signs, severe anaemia).
4. Initiate dolutegravir‑based ART (TDF + 3TC + DTG) as soon as HIV infection is confirmed; avoid NNRTI‑only regimens.
5. Give supportive care for toxin‑mediated disease: fluid resuscitation, monitor electrolytes, treat shock; consider antitoxin if locally available.
6. Monitor clinical response every 4‑6 h: fever curve, parasite clearance, CD4 trend, renal output, ECG for QT changes.
7. Escalate to referral centre if: parasitaemia ≥ 10 %, persistent coma, severe anaemia < 5 g/dL, QTc > 500 ms, or multi‑organ failure.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects of the core medicines and immediate actions to mitigate harm.
b: Artemether‑lumefantrine: may cause QT prolongation; obtain baseline ECG, avoid concomitant quinine or macrolides, correct hypokalaemia.
Dolutegravir: can raise serum creatinine by inhibiting tubular secretion; monitor renal function, do not stop if creatinine rise is <30 % without true AKI.
Quinine (if used): precipitates hypoglycaemia and cinchonism; give regular glucose checks, treat hypoglycaemia with 50 % dextrose, stop if severe tinnitus or visual disturbances.
Amphotericin B (for severe fungal toxin cases): nephrotoxicity and electrolyte loss; hydrate aggressively, replace potassium and magnesium, monitor daily creatinine.
Maraviroc (CCR5 blocker, rarely used): hepatotoxicity; obtain baseline LFTs, stop if transaminases >5 × ULN.

sections.p: Complications that signal treatment failure or impending organ damage and the criteria for urgent referral.
b: Persistent fever > 72 h despite antimalarial therapy → suspect drug resistance or secondary bacterial infection; refer.
Drop in haemoglobin > 2 g/dL within 24 h or absolute Hb < 5 g/dL → severe malaria anaemia; arrange blood transfusion and higher‑level care.
New onset seizures, coma, or respiratory distress in HIV‑positive patient → consider cerebral toxoplasmosis or cryptococcal meningitis; refer for lumbar puncture and antifungal therapy.
QTc prolongation > 500 ms on serial ECG while on quinine or artemisinin → stop offending drug, correct electrolytes, refer for cardiac monitoring.
Acute kidney injury (creatinine rise > 0.3 mg/dL in 48 h) during toxin management → stop nephrotoxic agents, give renal‑protective fluids, refer.

sections.p: How common co‑morbidities modify presentation, investigations and therapy.
b: HIV co‑infection: lowers CD4, increases susceptibility to severe malaria and bacterial sepsis; CD4 count guides prophylaxis, but start ART regardless of CD4.
Tuberculosis: may mimic fever and weight loss; obtain sputum GeneXpert if cough present; avoid rifampicin with dolutegravir without dose adjustment.
Malnutrition: blunts fever response, reduces drug absorption; give therapeutic feeds, consider higher‑dose oral artemisinin if vomiting persists.
Pregnancy: artemether‑lumefantrine safe in all trimesters; dolutegravir now recommended, avoid efavirenz in first trimester; monitor for anaemia.
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia worsens infection outcomes; check capillary glucose, treat with insulin if >250 mg/dL, avoid high‑dose quinine which can cause hypoglycaemia.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort): induce CYP enzymes, lower dolutegravir levels; counsel cessation.
Alcohol excess: potentiates quinine‑induced hypoglycaemia and hepatic toxicity; advise abstinence during treatment.
Renal or hepatic failure: adjust dosing of ART and antimalarials; prefer drugs with minimal hepatic metabolism (e.g., artesunate IV).

sections.p: Adaptations for children, pregnant women, the elderly and people living with HIV in low‑resource environments.
b: Children <5 years: use weight‑based artemisinin‑based combination therapy (artesunate + amodiaquine) if RDT unavailable; start dolutegravir‑based ART once weight > 10 kg, monitor growth.
Pregnancy: give artemether‑lumefantrine regardless of trimester; start dolutegravir‑based ART after first trimester or use TDF + 3TC + DTG throughout per WHO 2023 update.
Elderly (>65 y): higher risk of QT prolongation; obtain baseline ECG, avoid quinine if possible, monitor renal function closely.
People with HIV: prioritize integrase inhibitor‑based ART, screen for opportunistic infections, give cotrimoxazole prophylaxis; avoid drug–drug interactions with antimalarials.

Low‑resource settings: when microscopy unavailable, rely on WHO clinical severity criteria (e.g., impaired consciousness, respiratory distress) to start IV artesunate; use point‑of‑care CD4 or WHO staging for ART initiation.

facts: CD4+ T‑cell count <200 cells/µL defines AIDS and indicates severe membrane‑mediated HIV pathology.
Severe malaria: parasitaemia ≥5 % on peripheral smear or any sign of organ dysfunction mandates IV artesunate.
QTc prolongation >450 ms in men or >470 ms in women signals risk of torsades from quinine or other membrane‑active drugs.
Amphotericin B binds ergosterol; loss of membrane integrity leads to fungal cell death.
Dolutegravir‑based first‑line ART (TDF + 3TC + DTG) is WHO‑recommended for adults and pregnant women.
Artemether‑lumefantrine is the recommended artemisinin‑based combination therapy for all trimesters of pregnancy.
Hereditary elliptocytosis prevalence is highest among people of West African descent.
Sickle‑cell disease causes reduced red‑cell deformability; membrane rigidity leads to vaso‑occlusion.
CCR5 antagonists (e.g., maraviroc) are contraindicated in pregnancy and when virus uses CXCR4.
Rapid HIV test must be confirmed with a second, different rapid assay or laboratory test before diagnosis.

mnemonics.t: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol – first‑line TB drugs; often appears in membrane‑related exam questions.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a plateau in amino‑acid transport kinetics at high substrate concentration?
vivas.a: It indicates saturation of the carrier protein, reflecting a finite number of transporters (Vmax) and Michaelis‑Menten kinetics.

vivas.q: After steroid binds its intracellular receptor, what is the first intracellular event?
vivas.a: The receptor‑steroid complex undergoes a conformational change, dissociates from heat‑shock proteins, and translocates to the nucleus.

vivas.q: Which major class of antifungal drugs binds ergosterol and creates pores in the fungal cell membrane?
What is the correct statement about the fungal cell membrane?
vivas.a: Ergosterol is the primary sterol; its depletion compromises membrane fluidity and is targeted by azoles and polyenes.

vivas.q: Which antifungal class primarily targets membrane ergosterol?
vivas.a: Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis, while polyenes bind existing ergosterol.

vivas.q: What lipid does Amphotericin B bind to form lethal pores?
vivas.a: Ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane.

vivas.q: In which population is hereditary elliptocytosis most prevalent?
A 45‑year‑old man with a painless testicular mass shows cells with clear cytoplasm and distinct membranes; what tumour is most likely?
vivas.a: Seminoma, characterised by uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and prominent cell membranes.

vivas.q: Why is a single positive rapid HIV test insufficient for diagnosis?
vivas.a: Guidelines require a second, different rapid test or laboratory confirmation to avoid false‑positive results.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line ART regimen for an adult newly diagnosed with HIV in Kenya?
When artemisinin‑based therapy is unavailable for severe malaria, what alternative is acceptable?
vivas.a: Intravenous quinine with careful cardiac monitoring, recognizing its QT‑prolonging effect.

vivas.q: Which membrane channel is blocked by quinine causing QT prolongation?
vivas.a: The delayed rectifier potassium channel (IKr, hERG).

vivas.q: How can you differentiate HIV‑related membrane pathology from malaria‑induced red‑cell rigidity at the bedside?
vivas.a: HIV presents with opportunistic infections and CD4 decline; malaria shows fever, chills, and peripheral smear with parasites; membrane rigidity in malaria is inferred from severe anaemia and microvascular signs.

vivas.q: What bedside sign suggests severe malaria when rapid tests are unavailable?
vivas.a: Cerebral signs (altered consciousness) or severe anaemia (pallor, tachycardia) plus high parasitaemia on smear if possible.

vivas.q: Why are CCR5 antagonists unsuitable in pregnancy?
vivas.a: Safety data are limited and they may select for CXCR4‑tropic virus, risking treatment failure.

vivas.q: What is the key bedside test for detecting membrane‑related electrolyte disturbance in vomiting patients?
vivas.a: Assess for hypokalaemia: muscle weakness, flattened T waves on ECG, and check urine output.

vivas.q: What is the first step if a patient on quinine develops QT prolongation?
vivas.a: Stop quinine, correct electrolytes, and consider alternative antimalarial such as artesunate.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman with confirmed HIV presents with CD4 180 cells/µL. Which regimen should be started according to current Kenyan guidelines?
mcqs.e: Dolutegravir‑based regimen is first‑line for all adults regardless of CD4.

mcqs.q: A child with severe malaria cannot receive artemether‑lumefantrine due to stock‑out. Which drug is the recommended alternative?
mcqs.e: IV quinine is the WHO‑recommended alternative when artesunate is unavailable.

mcqs.q: Which antifungal class exerts its effect by inhibiting ergosterol synthesis rather than binding it?
mcqs.e: Azoles block the lanosterol 14‑α‑demethylase step, reducing ergosterol.

mcqs.q: A patient on quinine develops QTc 500 ms. Which ion channel is most likely affected?
Which sign is elicited by percussing the flank after the patient lies on their side, indicating free fluid in the abdomen?
mcqs.e: Shifting dullness occurs when fluid moves to the dependent flank, making it dull.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource setting, which bedside test helps differentiate hypokalaemia‑induced weakness from neuromuscular disease?
mcqs.e: Flattened or inverted T waves on ECG are classic for hypokalaemia.

cases.v: A 6‑year‑old boy from a rural Kenyan clinic presents with fever, chills, and dark urine. He is pale, tachycardic, and has a haemoglobin of 5 g/dL. Peripheral smear shows 6 % Plasmodium falciparum parasites with numerous ring forms.

qs.q: What is the immediate management step?
qs.a: Start intravenous artesunate promptly; if unavailable, give quinine IV with cardiac monitoring.

qs.q: Which membrane‑related complication explains his severe anaemia?
qs.a: Parasite‑induced rigidity and sequestration of infected red cells reduce deformability, leading to microvascular obstruction and haemolysis.

qs.q: If a rapid diagnostic test is out of stock, what bedside sign supports severe disease?
qs.a: Altered consciousness or respiratory distress together with pallor and high parasitaemia on smear.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old pregnant woman (first trimester) tests positive on an initial rapid HIV test. She reports no prior testing. Physical exam is unremarkable.

qs.q: What is the correct diagnostic algorithm?
qs.a: Perform a second, different rapid test for confirmation; if discordant, send a laboratory HIV‑1/2 immunoassay.

qs.q: Which antiretroviral regimen should be initiated?
qs.a: Tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir, as it is safe in all trimesters per WHO guidelines.

qs.q: Why is a CCR5 antagonist not appropriate here?
qs.a: Safety in pregnancy is not established and it is only useful when virus is CCR5‑tropic, which is unknown.

mistakes: Assuming a single positive rapid HIV test confirms infection without a second confirmatory test.
Prescribing NNRTI‑based first‑line ART instead of the current dolutegravir‑based regimen.
Using artemisinin‑based therapy in the first trimester without noting that artemether‑lumefantrine is actually safe.
Confusing the target of azoles (ergosterol synthesis) with polyenes (ergosterol binding).
Neglecting to monitor QT interval when giving quinine, leading to missed torsades risk.
Failing to recognise that severe malaria requires IV artesunate regardless of gestational age.
Prescribing CCR5 antagonists in pregnancy or without confirming viral tropism.
Over‑relying on rapid malaria tests when they are unavailable and not using peripheral smear or clinical severity signs.
